articles.title: Bridging Spiking and Continuous Dynamics in Spiking Neural Networks: A Muscle-Inspired Model
articles.summary: Transforming the spike trains produced by spiking neural networks (SNNs) into continuous signals through biologically inspired mechanisms remains an open challenge in generative and regression tasks.…
articles.abstract: Transforming the spike trains produced by spiking neural networks (SNNs) into continuous signals through biologically inspired mechanisms remains an open challenge in generative and regression tasks. In biological systems, a similar transformation occurs when muscles integrate neural spikes to produce smooth, coordinated movements. Inspired by this mechanism, we introduce a muscle-response model, a biologically motivated dynamical layer that converts spike trains into continuous representations. Our approach uses second-order dynamics to model the temporal integration of spiking activity. We investigate how the number of spiking neurons and temporal resolution affect the quality of the generated signals in a text-to-speech task, showing that increasing representational capacity has a greater impact than increasing temporal resolution under the evaluated configurations. Furthermore, an analysis of the learned dynamics reveals that, without explicit constraints on the response type, most neurons converge toward non-oscillatory behavior. These results demonstrate the potential of biologically inspired dynamical decoders for bridging spiking neural computation and continuous signal generation.

articles.title: OMCDE: Opposition-based Multi-Stage Matrix-Based Competitive Differential Evolution
articles.summary: Differential Evolution has proven to be an effective algorithm for continuous global optimization, but it's modern high-performing variants often introduce additional complexity and computational…
articles.abstract: Differential Evolution has proven to be an effective algorithm for continuous global optimization, but it's modern high-performing variants often introduce additional complexity and computational cost. We propose OMCDE, a matrix-based competitive Differential Evolution algorithm that aims to improve optimization performance while maintaining computational efficiency. The proposed approach integrates competition-driven search dynamics, adaptive behavior between optimization stages, and opposition-based initialization within a parallelizable framework. Empirical results on widely used CEC 2017 functions show that OMCDE achieves strong performance compared to several state-of-the-art DE algorithms, while remaining efficient and scalable. These findings indicate that OMCDE is a promising alternative for solving complex numerical optimization problems.

articles.title: Circuit Theory-Informed AI for Condition Monitoring in Power Electronics
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence for power electronics is evolving toward a deeper comprehension of system intrinsic behaviors and dynamics. As a novel integration of neural computation and electric circuits,…
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence for power electronics is evolving toward a deeper comprehension of system intrinsic behaviors and dynamics. As a novel integration of neural computation and electric circuits, spike-based neuromorphic computing offers promising potential in high energy efficiency and adaptability for data-driven applications. Building on the latency-coding principles, this article proposes a framework for data-light condition monitoring that relies solely on three-phase AC current measurements. The AC current signals are encoded as membrane potentials of RC-based spiking neurons, which are inherently compatible with spiking neural networks that can effectively facilitate the estimation of device parameters. Case studies are presented to validate the performances, while constraints and further optimizations are also evaluated and discussed, and future extensions of the methodology are provided.

articles.title: Two-Layer Evolutionary Scheduling for Machine Learning Jobs in Multi-Cluster Environments
articles.summary: The rapid growth of large-scale machine learning (ML) workloads has led to unprecedented demands on GPU cluster scheduling systems. However, existing heuristic schedulers struggle to handle the…
articles.abstract: The rapid growth of large-scale machine learning (ML) workloads has led to unprecedented demands on GPU cluster scheduling systems. However, existing heuristic schedulers struggle to handle the complexity and dynamics of multi-cluster GPU environments, often leading to load imbalance, long queuing delays, and poor alignment to business objectives. This paper formulates the ML scheduling problem in multi-cluster GPU environments as online multi-objective optimization that minimizes the average and maximum weighted queuing times while maximizing GPU time utilization. To solve this optimization problem, we propose EVO-GP, a two-layer evolutionary online scheduling method that decouples global job-to-cluster allocation from intra-cluster GPU resource allocation. At the job-to-cluster allocation layer, an evolutionary algorithm assigns arriving jobs to feasible clusters to promote load balance across clusters. At the resource allocation layer, a priority function automatically learned offline via genetic programming is used to rank jobs and guide GPU allocation within each cluster. Extensive experiments on both real-world data and simulated workloads demonstrate that the proposed EVO-GP method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, while maintaining superior adaptability and scalability.

articles.title: Robust Analysis of First-Price Auctions with Large Supply
articles.summary: This paper performs a robust analysis of welfare (i.e., the price of anarchy) in multi-unit first-price auctions with independent private values and unit-demand bidders. We employ a smoothness…
articles.abstract: This paper performs a robust analysis of welfare (i.e., the price of anarchy) in multi-unit first-price auctions with independent private values and unit-demand bidders. We employ a smoothness framework (see \citealp{ST-13}) to analyze the price of anarchy when supply is large. The main barrier to analysis in this framework is a worst-case bid distribution that establishes a lower bound on the price of anarchy of $1- \frac{1}{e}$. We show that such worst-case distributions cannot arise in equilibrium when agents' values satisfy a mild density lower bound condition. This characterization leads to novel asymptotic lower bounds. In particular, the price of anarchy for $ε$-approximate equilibrium as the number of units goes to infinity is at least $1-Θ\left(ε\log \left(\frac{1}ε\right)\right)$. Our analysis relies on a key structural property of equilibrium bid distributions: for a welfare analysis in any multi-unit first-price auction, it is without loss to analyze (approximate) equilibria with no atoms. In addition to this, we establish continuity and monotonicity properties of Bayes-Nash equilibria. We believe these results are of independent interest.

articles.title: Is Recursive Self-Improvement Safe?
articles.summary: The phrase recursive self-improvement (RSI) refers to the idea of an AI system designing and creating another, better AI system, which in turn designs and creates an even better one, and so on. While…
articles.abstract: The phrase recursive self-improvement (RSI) refers to the idea of an AI system designing and creating another, better AI system, which in turn designs and creates an even better one, and so on. While the idea has a long history, it has always been an abstract, futuristic idea -- until recently. Today's frontier AI has attained a set of abilities, including in programming, mathematics, research, tool use, and working coherently over extended periods of time, that make RSI seem plausible. AI companies are starting to pursue it, but many of the involved people are also expressing concerns, asking whether humanity should really set this in motion and under what conditions. I will discuss the situation, argue that we do not even have clear frameworks for thinking about the likely outcomes of RSI, and do a quick game-theoretic analysis of how to choose whether to initiate RSI when another party is making the same choice.

articles.title: FirstSwap: Pre-Consensus Trade Approvals for Decentralized Market Design
articles.summary: Decentralized exchanges typically give traders no execution guarantee until a block is finalized. In the meantime, external prices move, traders strategically delay submission, and block producers…
articles.abstract: Decentralized exchanges typically give traders no execution guarantee until a block is finalized. In the meantime, external prices move, traders strategically delay submission, and block producers can influence inclusion and ordering. We introduce FirstSwap, a DEX built on a constant-function market maker pricing curve that gives traders an early pre-approval before consensus, guaranteeing inclusion and execution within their submitted price limit, with final ordering determined by limit prices rather than by a block producer. We demonstrate the benefits of trade pre-approvals in an economic model combining auction theory with CEX-DEX arbitrage. When the CEX price changes gradually, FirstSwap rewards earlier traders with better prices, discouraging strategic delay and yielding higher social welfare and gains to AMM liquidity providers than a batch auction. When the CEX price jumps abruptly, FirstSwap yields higher welfare and smaller AMM losses than fair ordering. The central challenge is delivering fast trade pre-approvals without consensus. We introduce a decentralized, scaled admissibility protocol under which each validator reserves only a fraction of the available liquidity at every price. A trader obtains approval in a single round of messages with a quorum of validators. Somewhat surprisingly, despite Byzantine validators who may approve trades arbitrarily, we show that all quorum-certified trades are jointly admissible and execute within their limits. Our protocol extends naturally to a setting where buy and sell orders can be pre-approved against each other before a block is finalized.

articles.title: Proportionality in Elections under Feasibility Constraints and Ranked Ballots: The Solid Coalition Refinement Rule
articles.summary: We study elections with ranked ballots and general feasibility constraints, which indicate which sets of candidates are allowed as outcomes. We introduce the first proportionality axiom for this…
articles.abstract: We study elections with ranked ballots and general feasibility constraints, which indicate which sets of candidates are allowed as outcomes. We introduce the first proportionality axiom for this general setting and show that it extends the established notions from specific models that fit our general framework. We extend the Solid Coalition Refinement (SCR) rule to general constraints and prove that it satisfies our axiom exactly for matroid constraints. Although the naive implementation of SCR involves a step that is computationally intractable for weak orders, we show that in practical cases it can be implemented in polynomial time or efficiently in FPT time. We also illustrate limitations of this rule for approval ballots and provide its first empirical evaluation.

articles.title: Strategic Competition and Convergence in LLM Leaderboards
articles.summary: Leaderboards are a popular way to compare large language model (LLM) capabilities and can influence how model developers invest resources. We ask when competition on leaderboards leads developers to…
articles.abstract: Leaderboards are a popular way to compare large language model (LLM) capabilities and can influence how model developers invest resources. We ask when competition on leaderboards leads developers to produce models with similar capability profiles, which we call monoculture, or similar performance levels. We study this by formulating leaderboard competition as a game in which model developers invest resources across capabilities to maximize their win rate. We show that similar production functions can induce similar capability profiles, while comparative advantage can sustain distinct capability profiles. We then study convergence in performance levels and show that diminishing returns can lead to an increasingly crowded competitive frontier. Using data from LM Arena and OpenRouter, we find that developers improve more in categories where they lag competitors, while still retaining category-specific advantages. At the same time, we find that the frontier of models becomes increasingly crowded, alongside increasingly diversified model usage patterns. Our results suggest that increasing competition does not need to produce interchangeable models, but can instead sustain competitive models with distinct strengths.

articles.title: Contextual Search and Bilateral Trade with a Trace-Square-Root Potential
articles.summary: We present a unified potential method for contextual search and bilateral trade with one-bit feedback and obtain order-tight algorithms for both problems. Our framework starts from a Bayesian…
articles.abstract: We present a unified potential method for contextual search and bilateral trade with one-bit feedback and obtain order-tight algorithms for both problems. Our framework starts from a Bayesian perspective in which the unknown target (for contextual search) and the unknown pair of valuations (for bilateral trade) are sampled from a known prior distribution. In that model, the decision maker bases its prediction on the posterior distribution, obtained by conditioning on feedback received in previous rounds. For Bayesian contextual search, we present an algorithm with a total loss bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt Σ)$, where $Σ$ is the covariance matrix of the target's prior; and for contextual bilateral trade, our algorithm's regret is bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{Σ_S}+\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{Σ_B})$, where $Σ_S$ and $Σ_B$ are the covariance matrices of the seller's and buyer's valuations. We then use ideas from this Bayesian setting and adapt a ``dual'' of this trace-square-root potential to the classical worst-case setting, where the target and valuations are chosen adversarially from the unit Euclidean ball. For both contextual search and bilateral trade, we obtain tight $O(\sqrt d)$-regret algorithms. These results match the existing lower bounds up to a constant factor and improve on the previous guarantees of $O(d\log d)$ for contextual search and of $O(d6^d)$ for bilateral trade.

articles.title: Optimal Regret for Profit Maximization in Bilateral Trade
articles.summary: Learning to profit from trade requires learning both sides of a market: what a seller is willing to accept and what a buyer is willing to pay. We study repeated bilateral trade, where an intermediary…
articles.abstract: Learning to profit from trade requires learning both sides of a market: what a seller is willing to accept and what a buyer is willing to pay. We study repeated bilateral trade, where an intermediary posts a purchase price to a seller and a sale price to a buyer whose valuations are drawn from an unknown joint distribution. Trade occurs only if both parties accept their respective prices, in which case the intermediary earns the difference between the two prices. The intermediary observes only whether trade occurs, without observing either valuation. We show that learning both sides of the market is no harder, in terms of regret, than learning just one. Specifically, we design an algorithm achieving regret $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3})$ against the best fixed pair of prices, matching, up to logarithmic factors, the classical lower bound for one-dimensional dynamic pricing. Our result shows that the classical one-dimensional regret rate survives the transition to two dimensions, raising the question of whether this absence of a curse of dimensionality extends to arbitrarily high dimensions.

articles.title: Artificial Shoppers and Attention Competition
articles.summary: We study how AI shopping interfaces affect price competition, platform profit, and consumer welfare. A platform hosts two of three products of different quality.
articles.abstract: We study how AI shopping interfaces affect price competition, platform profit, and consumer welfare. A platform hosts two of three products of different quality. Without AI, consumers compare the hosted pair under salience distortion and overweight whichever attribute, price or quality, stands out. Under assistance, an AI assistant recommends the two products with the highest true utility, leaving consumers to make the same distorted comparison. Under delegation, an AI agent selects the best product, subject to purchase approval. Both modes access all products and know consumers' preferences; firms price strategically. First, assistance can soften competition despite expanded product access. The middle-quality firm may forgo low-valuation consumers because attracting them requires cutting the price paid by higher-valuation consumers as well. Relative to no AI with the same assortment, assistance lowers both hosted prices under the high- and low-quality pair but can raise both under the high- and middle-quality pair. Second, we identify an alignment paradox: some consumers can become worse off than without AI even though their best option remains recommended and becomes cheaper. Salience can induce a switch to a lower-quality product whose quality loss exceeds the saving relative to the original purchase. The assistant ranks products accurately but does not optimize the shortlist for consumers' realized welfare. Third, assistance can raise both platform profit and aggregate consumer surplus with the high- and middle-quality pair; delegation can do so with the high- and low-quality pair. Fourth, among AI designs, the platform weakly prefers delegation with the high- and middle-quality pair wherever all compared pricing equilibria exist. Yet this preferred design can yield lower platform profit and aggregate consumer surplus than the no-AI optimum.

articles.title: An Inspection Game for Monitor Design Against GNSS Timing Attacks in Synchronous Islanding
articles.summary: Phasor measurement units (PMUs) take their time from GNSS, so a spoofer that slowly drags a receiver clock rotates the reported phase without touching the power waveform. The threat is acute in…
articles.abstract: Phasor measurement units (PMUs) take their time from GNSS, so a spoofer that slowly drags a receiver clock rotates the reported phase without touching the power waveform. The threat is acute in synchronous islanding, where a controller keeps an islanded generator in phase with the grid, using one PMU on each side of an open breaker, so that the two can be reconnected at any moment: a differential clock bias of about $0.56$\,ms can make the controller hold the generator $10^\circ$ out of phase while it reports perfect synchronism. We cast the defense as a zero-sum inspection game. The defender, as inspector, chooses its timing monitors and audits the clocks periodically; the attacker, as inspectee, drags the two clocks to an unsafe bias by the next audit; the payoff is the evidence, the Kullback--Leibler divergence between the probability laws of the defender's record under attack and under normal operation. Our central result is that the evidence equals the cost of the cheapest innocent explanation of the attacked record. This single identity predicts which monitors work, turns the attacker's best response into a strictly convex quadratic program, and turns the defender's design into a convex program with a saddle point. Pairing explanations, which bound the evidence from above, with test statistics, which bound it from below, certifies audit periods in which every successful attack leaves at least a threshold of evidence. On a 50\,Hz island, these evidence-based periods, at the matched-test threshold, are up to 8.4 times as long as those of a rule that checks each monitor separately, and the case study favors placing the better oscillator on the utility side of the breaker.

articles.title: Attaining Optimal Values under Sure Constraints
articles.summary: A game may have, for each target below its value, a finite controller meeting that target, yet no finite controller attaining the value itself. We study finite stochastic games with a hard…
articles.abstract: A game may have, for each target below its value, a finite controller meeting that target, yet no finite controller attaining the value itself. We study finite stochastic games with a hard specification that must hold on every supported execution, including paths of probability zero. Max uses a pure finite controller; Min may use any pure public-history strategy. We distinguish three numerical questions: can a supplied target be met, can the unspecified optimum be attained, and what is one exact value? For explicit hard and Boolean soft Streett conditions, the strict and non-strict supplied-threshold problems are coNP-complete, attainment of the unsupplied supremum is $\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}$-complete, and one exact reduced fraction is $\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{NP}}$-complete under polynomial metric reductions. The proofs preserve both the value and its finite attainability when fixing a single opponent, and encode adaptive queries without computing unknown subgame values. The same construction yields matching value-comparison and exact-output lower bounds for ordinary stochastic Streett games with unrestricted randomized history strategies. We also bound the memory needed for optimal finite implementations for arbitrary Muller hard conditions and rational rewards in $[0,1]$ determined by infinitely recurring states. One controller is sure from the entire original sure region and attains at every finitely attained start, with no attainment premise on the other states. For $n$ states in that region it uses $2^{O(n\log(n+1))}Q(1+\log R)$ modes, where $Q$ is the product of the least common denominators of full original chance rows sourced in that sure region and $R$ clears all reward values. Its joint dependence on $Q$ and $R$ is worst-case sharp at each fixed $n\ge6$ when $Q,R\ge2$. Optimal dependence on arena size and efficient general synthesis are not resolved here.

articles.title: Fair Selection of Generalized Nash Equilibria: A Comparability Perspective
articles.summary: Generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problems model self-interested agents coupled through their costs and shared constraints, and arise throughout control applications that allocate a scarce common…
articles.abstract: Generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problems model self-interested agents coupled through their costs and shared constraints, and arise throughout control applications that allocate a scarce common resource. Such problems typically admit a continuum of equilibria, so any implementation must \emph{select} one. This selection is not neutral: it decides how the cost of the shared constraint is distributed among the agents, a decision often expected to be fair. The variational GNE (v-GNE), which charges all agents a uniform shadow price, is the conventional choice and is frequently advocated as fair. Through the lens of \emph{comparability} from social choice theory, we show that the GNE set itself requires no inter-agent comparability of costs, whereas the v-GNE implicitly assumes cardinal unit comparability, one of the stronger notions. We then introduce the fair GNE (f-GNE), which selects an equilibrium by explicitly optimizing a fairness metric matched to the comparability at hand, and give constructive routes to compute it for single-constraint and linear-quadratic games. An electric-vehicle charging game serves as a running example throughout this self-contained tutorial.

articles.title: As Easy as Rank One: Optimal Algorithms for Matroid Secretary and Single-Sample Matroid Prophet
articles.summary: We resolve the matroid secretary conjecture in its strong form and the single-sample matroid prophet inequality problem, achieving competitive ratios $e$ and $2$, respectively. Both ratios are…
articles.abstract: We resolve the matroid secretary conjecture in its strong form and the single-sample matroid prophet inequality problem, achieving competitive ratios $e$ and $2$, respectively. Both ratios are optimal, even for rank-one matroids. For matroid secretary, our ordinal algorithm accepts the elements of the canonical optimum independently, each with probability $1/e$. It needs only the number of elements in advance and uses an expected polynomial number of independence queries on arrived elements. For single-sample matroid prophet inequalities, our algorithm uses one sample per independent value distribution and $O(n^2)$ independence queries on a known $n$-element matroid. It works for every arrival order fixed independently of the samples, values, and algorithmic randomness. The selected elements and their values have exactly the joint distribution obtained by independently retaining each element--value pair in the canonical optimum of a fresh product draw with probability $1/2$. Our main algorithms maintain a reference state whose greedy solution contains every accepted element. Its updates, made even after rejections, preserve exact distributional invariants. A short reversible-update argument gives a $4$-probability-competitive secretary algorithm, already resolving the original conjecture; a related invariant gives the optimal single-sample prophet inequality. For secretary, we characterize the distributions achievable by ordinal algorithms through a finite polytope. A continuous-time formulation then lets us design an accepted-set distribution achieving the optimal ratio $e$ and realize it efficiently. We also obtain guarantees for matroid intersections.

articles.title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data
articles.summary: Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate identification of early disease markers. Manual data annotation is infeasible at…
articles.abstract: Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate identification of early disease markers. Manual data annotation is infeasible at population scale, motivating methods that automatically extract pre-defined phenotypes in multimodal and unstructured clinical data. Such pre-defined feature sets determine and limit which associations these approaches can discover. This limitation extends to agentic AI systems that use these tools to query population-scale data. In contrast, foundation models (FMs) trained on large volumes of clinical data can perform tasks beyond their training objectives. This suggests their latent embeddings may represent novel or unexplored features that could yield insights into disease mechanisms, yet such latent features remain difficult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce Glyph, an automated multistage framework that extracts features from multimodal and unstructured clinical data using FMs and sparse autoencoders, interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for clinical scientific discovery. We applied Glyph to abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports and laboratory measurements from 41,628 patients across different institutions. We identified 397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations. Moreover, a majority of discovered associations were automatically reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. Glyph concepts provided complementary associations to literature-derived markers, leading to gains in predictive power. We envision that interpretability can extend beyond a mechanistic understanding of neural networks to connecting implicitly learned features with clinical knowledge and establishing their significance for patient outcomes. We release Glyph at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph.

articles.title: Energy-Based Reasoners: Your Recurrent Reasoner Should Be an Energy-Based Model
articles.summary: Looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space.
articles.abstract: Looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345times less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance.

articles.title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design
articles.summary: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a…
articles.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0times higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://github.com/OpenBitSys/BitDecoding-FP4.

articles.title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
articles.summary: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the…
articles.abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.

articles.title: Invariance before structure: two modes of emergent compression in representation learning
articles.summary: Learned representations show striking invariance across biological and artificial neural networks, with different substrates and variations driven by drift, heterogeneity and initialisation. To…
articles.abstract: Learned representations show striking invariance across biological and artificial neural networks, with different substrates and variations driven by drift, heterogeneity and initialisation. To understand this invariance, we propose Emergent Adaptive Representation Learning (EARL), a framework that distinguishes two modes of emergence in learned representations: state-space compression, where a learned representation gains predictive power over its own future beyond what the network's units can predict individually, and parameter-space compression, where networks with different micro-level parameters converge to the same representation. We formalise both as Fisher sensitivities and introduce ensemble-level information-theoretic measures for each. In a recurrent reservoir with a trained bottleneck, parameter-space compression rises within the first few epochs of training and partly independently of the task, whereas state-space compression rises about 30 epochs later and only when the network begins to learn the temporal structure of the task. These results suggest that invariance to the substrate and task-specific emergent structure are acquired in distinct phases of learning.

articles.title: Projection-Free Gradient Tracking Neurodynamic for Distributed Nonnegative Sparse Optimization
articles.summary: This paper proposes a continuous-time, projection-free neurodynamic system based on gradient tracking for distributed nonnegative sparse optimization. Unlike traditional methods, our approach avoids…
articles.abstract: This paper proposes a continuous-time, projection-free neurodynamic system based on gradient tracking for distributed nonnegative sparse optimization. Unlike traditional methods, our approach avoids projecting states onto the feasible set. Instead, it employs gradient tracking to estimate average gradients under heterogeneous costs, coupling primal and dual dynamics such that feasibility and sparsity emerge naturally from the equilibrium conditions. The system ensures unique solutions through a locally Lipschitz vector field and guarantees that every equilibrium corresponds to an exact KKT point. We establish rigorous convergence guarantees for convex objectives through three distinct analytical layers. These include a centralized kernel rate, a computable distributed rate derived from Jacobian analysis without restrictive stability assumptions, and a global exponential stability proof based on Lur'e system theory. Our analysis quantitatively separates these layers, revealing that the convergence rate is primarily limited by graph sparsity and remains robust to variations in momentum time scales. Numerical experiments on strongly convex quadratic problems validate the theoretical rates, demonstrate effective active set recovery, and show that the system maintains stable tail convergence rates even under strong local heterogeneity.

articles.title: When Does Blockwise Additivity Break? Diagnosing and Repairing the Additive Assumption in Distillation-Based Architecture Search
articles.summary: Blockwise distillation methods for architecture search, such as DNA, DONNA, LANA and Puzzle, score each candidate replacement block in isolation and combine the scores additively. We ask at which…
articles.abstract: Blockwise distillation methods for architecture search, such as DNA, DONNA, LANA and Puzzle, score each candidate replacement block in isolation and combine the scores additively. We ask at which budgets this additivity assumption fails, whether fine-tuning repairs the failure, what diagnoses it, and how it can be repaired cheaply. On DeiT-S, DeiT-B, Swin-T and Qwen2.5-0.5B with seven latency budgets each, an additive integer program trails a pairwise interaction-aware program after fine-tuning by at most 1.6 top-1 points on ImageNet-1k at the mildest budgets, but by up to 17.5 points, and a factor of 1.9 in perplexity, at aggressive ones. After 10,000 fine-tuning steps 3.3-9.9 points remain on DeiT, whereas on Swin-T the gap shrinks to at most about 1.8 points within 500 steps. In a learning-rate sweep with the standard 2,000 steps, 6.0-10.7 points remain on DeiT when each method's rate is chosen by its evaluation-set accuracy. An intervention that keeps the block library and only forbids more than two removals in any three adjacent layers shrinks the DeiT gap from 5.8-17.5 to 0.7-5.2 points, mostly by improving the additive solution: adjacent removals are a major failure pattern. Splitting the additivity error into a metric and a functional part, relative to additive logit changes, indicates where a cheap logit-sum predictor can be trusted. A hybrid search that ranks moves with this predictor and measures only the best needs no pair measurements and, after Holm adjustment, is significantly better than the pairwise program in 10 of 14 ImageNet-1k settings, with no statistically significant losses. An ablation shows that its ranking helps except at the most aggressive DeiT-B budget, where the predictor misleads and random ranking or ten-times-costlier evolution does better.

articles.title: Optimal Contention Resolution from Samples
articles.summary: Contention resolution schemes convert random sets which are ex-ante feasible for some constraint into sets which are feasible ex post, and their online variants have broad applications in Bayesian…
articles.abstract: Contention resolution schemes convert random sets which are ex-ante feasible for some constraint into sets which are feasible ex post, and their online variants have broad applications in Bayesian and stochastic optimization, including prophet inequalities and stochastic probing. In many such applications, however, full distributional knowledge is an unattainable requirement. This motivates the study of contention resolution schemes which employ a limited number of samples from the underlying distributions. We study sample-based contention resolution for $k$-uniform matroids, for both uniformly random and adversarial arrival orders, and compare their balance guarantees to the best possible with full distributional knowledge. For a single-item constraint, we show that one sample per element suffices for an optimal $(1-1/e)$-balanced ROCRS. For adversarial arrivals, however, we prove that no single-sample OCRS can be $1/2$-balanced, even for known arrival orders, separating contention resolution from prophet inequalities in the single-sample setting. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that two samples are necessary and sufficient for the optimal $1/2$ guarantee. We also present a single-sample $0.48$-balanced scheme. For general $k$, we give a simple single-sample ROCRS that achieves an optimal balance ratio of $1-e^{-k}k^k/k!$. In adversarial order, we obtain a single-sample $(1 - O(1/\sqrt{k}))$-balanced scheme, matching the optimal asymptotic dependence on $k$. Finally, we complete the picture by characterizing the minimum number of samples needed to match the optimal balance ratio achievable with full distributional knowledge. For random arrivals, one sample suffices for $k = 1,2,3,4$, and zero samples suffice for $k \geq 5$. For an adversarial arrival order, even known in advance, and any $k \geq 2$, we show that no constant number of samples suffices to achieve optimal balance.

articles.title: Information Elicitation by Ordinal Agreement
articles.summary: Ordinal information is central to tasks ranging from conference peer review to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback for large language models. In many such settings, there is no objective…
articles.abstract: Ordinal information is central to tasks ranging from conference peer review to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback for large language models. In many such settings, there is no objective ground truth against which reports can be directly verified, making incentive-compatible elicitation challenging. Peer-prediction mechanisms have been designed to achieve truthful elicitation despite the lack of ground-truth verification. However, existing peer-prediction methods do not provide incentives for agents to truthfully compress rich private information (e.g. reviews) into coarser ordinal reports (e.g. rankings) requested by the mechanisms. We propose a simple ordinal peer-prediction mechanism that rewards agents based on pairwise agreement, measured by Kendall tau. Under a broad class of Bayesian Stochastically Order Consistent models---which includes classical models such as Mallows and Thurstone---we prove that truthful reporting is stochastically dominant, and strongly truthful under index-equivariant strategies. This provides robust incentives even for agents with non-linear utility functions, such as risk aversion. Our mechanism further accommodates heterogeneous agents, top-K reports, and subset assignments, where each agent is scored against one randomly drawn peer. Experiments on synthetic Mallows and Thurstone data, together with a real-data stress test on the SUSHI preference dataset, show right-shifted truthful-payment distributions and the highest normalized sensitivity among tested baselines.

articles.title: Regret Bounds for Profit Maximization in Bilateral Trade: Learning the Best Posted-Price Mechanism
articles.summary: Bilateral trade models the task of intermediating between two strategic agents, a seller and a buyer, willing to trade a good for which they hold private valuations. We study this problem from the…
articles.abstract: Bilateral trade models the task of intermediating between two strategic agents, a seller and a buyer, willing to trade a good for which they hold private valuations. We study this problem from the perspective of a profit-maximizing broker in a regret minimization framework. At each time step, a new seller and buyer arrive and the broker proposes a trading price to each agent. The trade happens if both agents accept, and the profit of the broker is the difference between the price received from the buyer and the one paid to the seller. At the end of each interaction, the learner only observes whether the trade occurred, and its goal is to achieve sublinear regret relative to the best fixed pair of prices in hindsight. We start by investigating the adversarial version of the problem, where buyer and seller valuations are generated by an adversary. In this setting, we construct a polynomial-time learning algorithm with a $\tilde O(T^{\frac 23})$ regret rate, which is nearly tight even if the valuations are drawn i.i.d. from independent distributions, thus matching the rate for one-sided pricing. Our adversarial algorithm combines a localized estimation procedure with an information-based minimax construction. We then consider valuations drawn i.i.d. from independent distributions satisfying the monotone-hazard-rate (MHR) property and provide a learning algorithm with nearly tight $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret. The algorithm combines localized estimation with a stochastic convex bandit routine applied to the negative logarithm of expected profit. Finally, we complement this result by showing a separation between MHR and regular distributions, proving that the minimax regret rate in the latter setting is $\tilde Θ(T^{\frac 35})$. This last result contrasts with the $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret bound that can be obtained for one-sided pricing with regular distributions.

articles.title: Distributed Optimization Involving Non-Lipschitzian, Linear Composite Functions: Unified Algorithm Design and Convergence Analysis
articles.summary: This paper formulates a generic distributed nonsmooth optimization problem subject to edge-based equality constraints, local inequality constraints characterized by general convex functions, as well…
articles.abstract: This paper formulates a generic distributed nonsmooth optimization problem subject to edge-based equality constraints, local inequality constraints characterized by general convex functions, as well as globally coupling constraints including affine equality and nonlinear inequality. The terminal goal is to minimize the sum of local non-differentiable convex functions and proximable nonsmooth convex composite terms attached to linear operators, over networked multi-agent systems. This formulated framework not only applies in complex practical problems but also reduces to existing distributed optimization structures. To cope with technical issues caused by local linear mappings, potential multiple nonsmooth functions and coupling nonlinear constraints, we first derive a new local first-order condition, and further present a novel fully distributed optimization algorithm based on variable decompositions and proximal operators. Specifically, the proposed algorithm allows each agent to update states via local information exchange and through {locally fixed step-sizes}, and to find inexact solutions of subproblems without loss of convergence speed. In contrast to existing tailor-made algorithms for the bounded gradients of objective functions or affine constraints, our algorithm is capable of solving more practical cases involving general convex functions and nonlinear constraints. Under mild assumptions, the convergence rate $o(1/k)$ in terms of the optimality and successive-difference metrics is achieved, by constructing the equivalent variational inequalities of the proposed algorithm. Finally, numerical experiments on practical application problems illustrate the theoretical results.

articles.title: Learning and Steering in Incomplete-Information Games
articles.summary: In many modern multi-agent systems, a mediator seeks to influence strategic decision dynamics using only outcome-level feedback and without knowing agents' utilities. In this work, we study how a…
articles.abstract: In many modern multi-agent systems, a mediator seeks to influence strategic decision dynamics using only outcome-level feedback and without knowing agents' utilities. In this work, we study how a mediator can learn an unknown game and steer adaptive agents toward outcomes that maximize her utility using only trajectory feedback. The mediator knows the game form and her own objective, but not the agents' utilities. Moreover, she commits to nonnegative payments and provides recommendations and contexts, but receives only a single realized terminal outcome rather than full-information feedback. We develop halving-type algorithms that learn utility differences in normal-form games and conditional continuation-value differences in extensive-form games, achieving a sample complexity of $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ that matches worst-case lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. We then combine these learning procedures with a Lagrangian formulation in an online Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm that interleaves learning, equilibrium computation, and steering toward mediator-optimal extensive-form correlated equilibria (EFCE). With high probability, the Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm achieves a directness gap and an optimality gap of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/4})$, while time-average payments are of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/8})$.

articles.title: Cores of $3$-distant convex games
articles.summary: Convex cooperative games have a nonempty core and admit an efficient construction of core allocations. However, economically natural local frictions may violate convexity.
articles.abstract: Convex cooperative games have a nonempty core and admit an efficient construction of core allocations. However, economically natural local frictions may violate convexity. We study the core of $3$-distant convex games, which permit violations of convexity only between closely related coalitions. Although the core of such a game may be empty, we establish a simple necessary and sufficient condition for its nonemptiness. We also develop a strongly polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm for finding a core allocation whenever one exists. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of the framework to oligopolistic competition with merger synergies and profit allocation of joint production with complementary inputs.

articles.title: Transparency in Team Contracts
articles.summary: In contract design, the principal is often better informed about the project's chances of succeeding than the agents. To incentivize effort, the principal has two main tools: first, to design a…
articles.abstract: In contract design, the principal is often better informed about the project's chances of succeeding than the agents. To incentivize effort, the principal has two main tools: first, to design a contract, sharing part of the project's success among the agents; second, to design a (Bayesian) persuasion scheme, selectively sharing information with the agents. In this work we are interested in the optimal combination of both these tools. We tackle the joint problem through the prism of simplicity vs. optimality, and establish a stark dichotomy: The simple disclosure scheme of full transparency achieves a tight $4/3$-approximation to the optimal combination of information disclosure and team contract, when the team's production function is submodular. In contrast, full transparency can be arbitrarily far from optimal when production is supermodular. The techniques that we develop to bound the gap for submodular functions, also yield a new deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm for pure multi-agent contract design, with a significantly improved approximation ratio of $2.311$, and thus a $3.081$-approximation algorithm for the joint information and contracting problem.

articles.title: Polynomial-Time Approximate EFX for Chores via Flow and Matching
articles.summary: We study approximate EFX allocations of indivisible chores under nonnegative additive costs. Exact EFX allocations need not exist in general.
articles.abstract: We study approximate EFX allocations of indivisible chores under nonnegative additive costs. Exact EFX allocations need not exist in general. We develop a polynomial-time algorithm that computes a complete $(3+\varepsilon)$-EFX allocation for any rational $0<\varepsilon\leq1$, improving the previous approximation guarantee from a factor depending on the number of agents to a constant. The algorithm extends to EF$k$X, achieving a $(2+1/k+\varepsilon)$-approximation for every integer $k\geq1$. For instances with relatively few chores, the polynomial-time BRBI algorithm gives stronger guarantees. It finds exact EF$k$X allocations when $m\leq2kn$ and achieves a factor of at most $2-1/k$ when $m\le(3k-1)n$. In particular, $k=1$ and $m\leq2n$ give exact EFX. We further show that the approximation factor \(2+1/k\) is asymptotically tight for our main algorithm. We also construct a four-agent, ten-chore instance in which every complete allocation has EFX approximation factor at least $11/10$, improving upon the $20/19$ lower bound for submodular costs even under additive costs.
